hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of a young bean seedling growing in a clear glass jar on a sunny classroom windowsill, with fine white root hairs, a stiff green stem and two flat green leaves, and a blue sky outside the window.
hero.alt: A bean seedling in a glass jar on a sunny windowsill, showing white root hairs, a green stem and flat green leaves.

slides.title: Do plant cells specialise too?
slides.subtitle: Look at the bean seedling. Sketch one root cell and one leaf cell, and label what each does.
slides.time_note: 3 minutes of silent sketching and writing, plus a short set-up

blocks.text: A bean seedling in a jar with white root hairs, a green stem and flat green leaves.
items: bean_seedling_windowsill

A friendly flat cartoon of a young bean seedling growing in a clear glass jar on a sunny classroom windowsill, with fine white root hairs, a stiff green stem and two flat green leaves, and a blue sky outside the window.

blocks.text: Do plant cells also specialise? What might a root-tip cell look like compared with a leaf cell?

do: Display the class bean seedling at the front, where everyone can see it.
Point to the three regions: the fine white root hairs, the stiff stem and the flat green leaves.
Remind learners that blood cells specialise: platelets are flat and sticky, red blood cells are disc-shaped.
Set a visible 3-minute timer. Learners work alone and in silence in their notebooks.
Circulate. Note which shapes learners draw and which words they use. Do not correct anything.
If anyone handles the seedling, they wash their hands afterwards. Check first that no learner has a legume allergy. Keep microscope slides from earlier lessons stored away.
say: Before I show you anything, I want your brain's best guess.
Look carefully at this seedling: the root hairs, the stem, the leaf.
You have 3 minutes of silence to sketch and write.
notes.wait_time: 3 minutes of silent writing. Stay silent yourself.
look_for: Every learner has a sketch and at least one written label within the 3 minutes. Check at least 8 notebooks.
Note, without correcting, who draws long thin shapes and who draws round shapes.
Note who mentions chloroplasts or surface area. This shows how well learners transfer ideas from the animal cell lessons.
if_then: If a learner is stuck, say: 'Think about blood cells. Their shape fitted their job. What jobs do roots and leaves do?'
If a learner writes 'all plant cells are the same', say: 'Write why you think so. Now look at the root and the leaf. Do they do the same job?'
notes.why_this_works: Committing an idea to paper before any teaching activates what learners know about blood cells and gives them a hook for later. The common misconception is that only animals have specialised cells; this slide lets learners commit to an idea so the class can test it.
answer_key: Learners' own reasoned ideas are acceptable. Model answer: 'Yes, plant cells specialise. A root cell may be long and thin so it can take in water from the soil. A leaf cell may be tall and full of green chloroplasts so it can catch light and make food.'

slides.title: Share with your partner
slides.subtitle: Show your sketches. Explain why you drew them that way.
slides.time_note: Pair talk: 1 minute

blocks.text: What did you predict, and why?

items: people :: Turn to your shoulder partner
eyes :: Show your two sketches
speech :: Say what each cell does and why

do: Say when to start. Start the 1-minute timer.
Learners work in shoulder pairs. Both partners speak.
Listen to three pairs. Do not correct.
say: Turn to your partner and share your sketches.
Tell your partner what you think each cell does, and why.
look_for: Both partners in each pair are speaking.
Listen for reasons that use shape or job, not only 'because'.
if_then: If a pair finishes early, say: 'Find one difference between your two sketches. Which idea do you trust more, and why?'
If a pair has nothing to say, say: 'Read each other's labels aloud. Do you agree with them?'
notes.why_this_works: Talking to a partner first lets every learner rehearse an idea in a safe space. Learners are then more willing to share with the whole class.

slides.title: BEFORE — Our Predictions
slides.subtitle: Four voices. No corrections yet.
slides.time_note: Cold-call 4 learners, 12 seconds of wait time each

items: Root cell ideas :: What do we think a root cell looks like?
Leaf cell ideas :: What do we think a leaf cell looks like?

blocks.text: What did you predict the root cell looks like, and why?

do: Draw two columns on the board: 'Root cell ideas' and 'Leaf cell ideas'. Title the board 'BEFORE — Our Predictions'.
Use name cards to cold-call exactly 4 learners.
Choose at least one learner who said 'yes, they specialise' and one who is uncertain. Use what you saw while circulating.
Write every prediction on the board word for word. Do not correct errors.
say: What did you predict the root cell looks like, and why?
Thank you. Hold onto these predictions. We will come back and see who was closest to what biologists actually found.
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after each question before taking an answer
look_for: All 4 predictions are on the board in the right column, word for word.
At least one 'yes' voice and one uncertain voice were heard.
Listen for reasons that mention surface area, chloroplasts or shape.
if_then: If a learner cannot answer after 12 seconds, say: 'Talk to your partner for 10 seconds. I will come back to you.'
If an answer is wrong, say: 'Thank you. We will test that idea soon.' Write it on the board without comment.
If all four say 'yes', ask: 'Does anyone have a different idea, or a question?'
notes.why_this_works: A public record of ideas, with no corrections, makes learners feel safe to be wrong. It also gives the class something real to check in the Explain phase.

slides.title: How we study each cell
slides.subtitle: Five cells. The same steps each time. Rule five rows in your book.
slides.time_note: Set up the observation table before the first cell

items: eyes :: Look in silence for 30 seconds
pencil :: Draw and label the cell
memo :: Fill in one row of the table

rows: What I think it helps the cell do

do: Learners rule the 3-column table in their notebooks with 5 empty rows (the slide shows only 2). They leave space for five drawings.
Explain the routine: silent looking, then drawing, then one table row.
Tell learners they record only what they can see in the diagram, then make a careful guess about what it helps the cell do.
say: For each cell, study the diagram in silence for 30 seconds before you draw anything.
Notice the shape, the thickness of the walls and what is inside.
Then write what you can see, and what you think it helps the cell do.
look_for: Check 5 notebooks: the table has the three column headings and room for five rows.
if_then: If learners ask for the right answer, say: 'First tell me what you can see. Then make your best guess about the job.'
notes.why_this_works: A three-column table makes learners move from seeing to inferring on every cell. This stops them copying a diagram without thinking.
answer_key: Table format: Cell name | Key structural features I can see | What I think this helps the cell do. Model first row: Root hair cell | long tube-like extension (root hair), large vacuole, thin cell wall, no chloroplasts | the long extension gives a large surface to take in water and mineral salts.

slides.title: Cell 1: Root hair cell
slides.subtitle: Look in silence first. Then draw, label and fill in row 1.
slides.time_note: 30 seconds silent looking, then drawing and one table row

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph. A root hair cell.
What is the most unusual feature of this cell compared with a basic plant cell?

do: Show the diagram. Start the 30-second silent timer.
After 30 seconds, learners draw and label the cell, then fill in row 1.
Circulate and ask the question on the slide to learners who are stuck.
Do not say what the cell does. Learners guess first.
say: Study this diagram in silence for 30 seconds before you draw anything.
Notice the shape, the thickness of the walls and what is inside.
What is the most unusual feature of this cell compared with a basic plant cell?
look_for: Check 6 notebooks: at least two structural features and one function guess that uses structural evidence.
Look for a drawing that shows the long root hair and is large enough to label.
if_then: If a learner writes only 'it has a root hair', say: 'What does the root hair do to the surface of the cell? What could that help with?'
If a learner draws a tiny cell, say: 'Use half a page so your labels fit.'
notes.why_this_works: Silent looking before drawing makes learners notice details. The common misconception is that every plant cell looks the same; the unusual feature question points to what is different here.
answer_key: Row 1: Root hair cell | long tube-like extension (root hair); large vacuole; thin cell wall; no chloroplasts | the long thin root hair gives a large surface area to take in water and mineral salts from the soil.

slides.title: Cell 2: Guard cells
slides.subtitle: Look in silence first. Then draw, label and fill in row 2.
slides.time_note: 30 seconds silent looking, then drawing and one table row

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph. A pair of guard cells.
What is the most unusual feature of these cells?

do: Show the diagram. Start the 30-second silent timer.
Learners draw and label, then fill in row 2.
Circulate and ask the question on the slide.
say: Study this diagram in silence for 30 seconds before you draw anything.
What is the most unusual feature of these cells compared with a basic plant cell?
look_for: Check 5 notebooks: kidney shape, thick inner wall, chloroplasts and the central pore are noticed.
At least one function guess that uses structure.
if_then: If a learner writes 'it makes food' only, say: 'Which part of the drawing is the pore? What could the two cells do to the pore?'
notes.why_this_works: Comparing each new cell with a basic plant cell trains learners to look for what is different, which is the key skill for linking structure to function.
answer_key: Row 2: Guard cells | kidney-shaped pair; thick inner wall; chloroplasts present; central pore (stoma) | the pair can change shape to open or close the stoma, so they control how much water leaves the leaf.

slides.title: Guard cells in two places
slides.subtitle: Compare stomata in a dry place and a humid place.
slides.time_note: Look, show fingers, then record in your table

items: Turkana (dry) :: Maize leaf. Look at the stomata.
Kericho (humid) :: Tea leaf. Look at the stomata.

blocks.text: How open are the stomata in each place? What might the guard cells be doing differently?

do: Show the two stomatal images side by side: a maize leaf from dry Turkana and a tea leaf from humid Kericho. You must supply these images.
Ask for a vote on fingers: 1 for Turkana, 2 for Kericho. Which location has guard cells that are more open?
Wait 10 seconds before they show fingers.
Learners record what they see in row 2 of their table or the margin. They record only what they see.
say: What do you notice about how open the stomata are in each location?
Show me on your fingers: 1 for Turkana, 2 for Kericho. In which location are the guard cells more open?
What might the guard cells be doing differently?
look_for: Count the fingers. Most learners should show 2 (Kericho).
Check 5 notebooks: learners write what they see, then a link to guard cell action.
Listen for the idea that guard cells respond to the environment.
if_then: If many show 1, say: 'Look at the size of the gap between the guard cells in each picture. Which gap is wider?'
If a learner says 'the plant is thirsty', say: 'Good. What would the guard cells do to the stoma to save water?'
notes.why_this_works: A local contrast makes the guard cell job real for Kenyan learners. The common misconception is that stomata are open the same amount everywhere; the two pictures challenge this.
answer_key: Observation: In dry Turkana the stomata are mostly closed. In humid Kericho they are mostly open. Idea: guard cells close the stomata in dry places to reduce water loss, and open them more in humid places.

slides.title: Cell 3: Xylem vessel
slides.subtitle: Look in silence first. Then draw, label and fill in row 3.
slides.time_note: 30 seconds silent looking, drawing, then a short class link

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph. A xylem vessel.
What is the most unusual feature of this cell?

do: Show the diagram. Start the 30-second silent timer.
Learners draw and label, then fill in row 3.
Circulate. Check how learners describe the inside of the cell.
Then ask the class the question about the fibroblast, as in the Say lines.
say: Study this diagram in silence for 30 seconds before you draw anything.
Remember the fibroblast. It had lots of rough ER to make collagen.
The xylem vessel gave up its entire living contents to become a hollow pipe. Both cells sacrificed something to do a job.
What does that tell us about specialisation?
notes.wait_time: 30 seconds of silent looking; 10 seconds after the specialisation question
look_for: Check 6 notebooks: at least two features (hollow lumen, thick lignified wall) and a function guess.
Check that xylem is NOT described as 'alive' or 'has cytoplasm'. This is a common misconception to address in Explain.
if_then: If a learner draws a nucleus or cytoplasm, say: 'Look at the labels. What is inside this cell? Is it full or empty?'
If a learner writes only 'it is hollow', say: 'Why would a hollow tube help something to flow through?'
notes.why_this_works: Linking the xylem to the fibroblast shows that specialisation can mean giving something up. The slide targets the misconception that all cells must contain living cytoplasm.
answer_key: Row 3: Xylem vessel | hollow lumen; thick lignified wall; no end walls; no living cytoplasm | water can flow through the hollow tube easily, and the thick wall keeps the tube open.
notes.science_note: Lignin is the hard material in the xylem wall. It makes the wall strong.

slides.title: Cell 4: Phloem sieve tube
slides.subtitle: Look in silence first. Then draw, label and fill in row 4.
slides.time_note: 30 seconds silent looking, then drawing and one table row

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph. A phloem sieve tube with a companion cell.
What is the most unusual feature of this cell?

do: Show the diagram. Start the 30-second silent timer.
Learners draw and label, then fill in row 4.
Circulate and ask the question on the slide.
say: Study this diagram in silence for 30 seconds before you draw anything.
What is the most unusual feature of this cell compared with a basic plant cell?
look_for: Check 5 notebooks: thin walls, sieve plates (holes) at the ends, companion cell alongside.
At least one function guess that uses the sieve plate.
if_then: If a learner writes 'it carries things', say: 'What is special about the ends of the cell? What could pass through them?'
notes.why_this_works: Asking learners to name the single most unusual feature focuses attention on structure that links directly to function.
answer_key: Row 4: Phloem sieve tube | thin walls; sieve plates (holes) at the ends; a companion cell alongside | the holes in the sieve plates let sugar pass from one cell to the next along the tube.

slides.title: Cell 5: Palisade mesophyll cell
slides.subtitle: Look in silence first. Then draw, label and fill in row 5.
slides.time_note: 30 seconds silent looking, then drawing and one table row

blocks.text: This is a drawing, not a photograph. A palisade mesophyll cell from a leaf.
What is the most unusual feature of this cell?

do: Show the diagram. Start the 30-second silent timer.
Learners draw and label, then fill in row 5.
Circulate and ask the question on the slide.
say: Study this diagram in silence for 30 seconds before you draw anything.
What is the most unusual feature of this cell compared with a basic plant cell?
look_for: Check 5 notebooks: tall cylindrical shape, many chloroplasts, large central vacuole.
At least one function guess that uses the chloroplasts.
if_then: If a learner writes 'it is green', say: 'Why is green useful? What do chloroplasts do for a leaf?'
notes.why_this_works: By the fifth cell, learners can use the same routine on their own. This builds the habit of reading structure as evidence of function.
answer_key: Row 5: Palisade mesophyll cell | tall cylindrical shape; many chloroplasts packed in; large central vacuole | the many chloroplasts trap light for photosynthesis, so the cell can make a lot of food.

slides.title: Which cell surprised you?
slides.subtitle: Say which cell surprised you, and exactly why.
slides.time_note: Cold-call 3 learners; 12 seconds of wait time each

items: seedling :: Root hair cell
door :: Guard cells
droplet :: Xylem vessel
arrow_down :: Phloem sieve tube
leaf :: Palisade cell

blocks.text: Which of these five cells surprised you the most? What surprised you?

do: Cold-call 3 learners with name cards. Choose one who wrote strong function guesses, one who found the table hard, and one who has not spoken yet.
While they think, check that tables are complete: five rows, two features and one function guess per cell.
Do not give the full explanation yet. That comes in Explain.
say: Which of these five cells surprised you the most, and what specifically surprised you?
Thank you. Keep your table. We will use it to check our predictions.
look_for: Check 8 tables: at least two features and one function guess for each cell, using structural evidence.
Listen for 'specifically' answers that name a feature, not just a cell.
if_then: If a learner says 'all of them', say: 'Pick one. What was the feature that made you say that?'
If a learner cannot answer, say: 'Look at your drawing of the xylem. What do you see that a basic plant cell has, but this one does not?'
notes.why_this_works: A short sharing round lets the teacher hear how learners reason before any explanation. The common misconception is that plants have only a few simple cell types; learners see five very different ones.

slides.title: Match the cards
slides.subtitle: Groups of four. Match 15 cards into 5 sets of 3: diagram, function, place.
slides.time_note: 8 minutes for matching

items: F1 · Carries water up the plant
F2 · Makes food by photosynthesis
F3 · Absorbs water and mineral salts from the soil
F4 · Opens and closes the stoma
F5 · Carries sugars around the plant
C1 · Roots, stem, leaf veins; beside a companion cell
C2 · Outer layer of roots, just behind the tip
C3 · Leaves: more open in humid Kericho, more closed in dry Turkana
C4 · Just below the upper surface of the leaf
C5 · Roots, stem, leaf veins; no end walls

do: Before class, prepare 15 cards per group: 5 unlabelled cell diagram cards (copy the five drawings from Observe without labels), 5 function cards (F1-F5) and 5 place cards (C1-C5).
Make groups of four. Give each group one set of cards.
Say that no card is used twice and every member must be able to explain every match.
Start the 8-minute timer. Circulate and listen to the reasons groups give.
If you have few card sets, groups can share a projected set and write the matches in their books.
say: You have 8 minutes to match all 15 cards into 5 sets of 3.
No card is used twice.
Every group member must be able to explain every match, not just the one you made yourself.
look_for: Groups give reasons that use structure, such as 'long extension', 'hollow', 'holes at the ends'.
Note which cell is matched wrongly most often. Record it for the teacher reflection.
if_then: If a group is stuck, say: 'Pick the cell you are most sure about. Which function card fits its shape?'
If a group matches by guessing, say: 'Show me the feature on the diagram that tells you this match.'
notes.why_this_works: Handling the cards lets learners test ideas with their hands before they must explain in words. Common misconception: matching by cell name only; the 'explain every match' rule stops this.
answer_key: Root hair cell: F3 and C2.
Guard cells: F4 and C3.
Xylem vessel: F1 and C5.
Phloem sieve tube: F5 and C1.
Palisade mesophyll cell: F2 and C4.

slides.title: Freeze! Hold up a set
slides.subtitle: Hold up your set for the root hair cell.
slides.time_note: Quick check of all groups

blocks.text: Hold up the 3 cards that match the root hair cell.
items: Be ready to explain your reasoning.

do: Say 'Freeze'. Groups stop moving cards.
Scan all groups quickly for the root hair set. Look for errors.
Choose one group with an error and ask them to explain.
Check the other four sets with the answer key as time allows.
say: Freeze. Each group, hold up your set for the root hair cell.
Walk me through your reasoning for that match.
notes.wait_time: 12 seconds after the question to the chosen group
look_for: Count how many groups have the correct set (diagram, F3, C2).
Note whether any group mismatched xylem or phloem. If more than one third of groups did, plan a 5-minute re-teach at the start of Lesson 10.
if_then: If a group is wrong, say: 'Which feature of the root hair cell would help it do that job? Look at the diagram again.'
If every group is correct, say: 'Now tell me which card was hardest to match, and why.'
notes.why_this_works: A fast whole-class check shows the teacher where understanding is weak before the explanations begin. Choosing a group with an error makes learners explain, not just guess.
answer_key: Root hair cell set: the root hair cell diagram, F3 (Absorbs water and mineral salts from the soil) and C2 (Outer layer of roots, just behind the tip).

slides.title: Explain your cell: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning
slides.subtitle: Pick one cell. One spokesperson speaks for 90 seconds.
slides.time_note: Short preparation, then 90-second presentations

items: Claim :: This is a … cell.
Evidence :: I can see …
Reasoning :: This means it can …
hand :: Thumbs up = I agree with the reasoning
raised_hand :: Flat hand = I need more evidence

do: Each group chooses one cell and prepares a 90-second explanation using the Claim, Evidence, Reasoning frame.
One spokesperson presents. Time each presentation.
Make sure different cells are covered. Choose groups for cells not yet presented.
The class gives a hand signal after each presentation: thumbs up or flat hand.
say: Choose one cell. Use the frame: Claim, Evidence, Reasoning.
The claim names the cell. The evidence is what you can see. The reasoning says how that helps the job.
Thumbs up if you agree with the reasoning. Flat hand if you need more evidence.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each presentation before the hand signal
look_for: Each presentation names a structural feature as evidence, not just a function label.
Count flat hands. Ask those learners what evidence is missing.
if_then: If a group gives only the function, say: 'What can you SEE on the diagram that tells us this?'
If the class shows flat hands, say: 'What evidence would make you agree?'
If time runs out, tell groups you will hear the other cells next lesson.
notes.why_this_works: The frame makes the form-and-function logic clear, so learners can use it for any cell. The common misconception is that function labels are enough; the evidence step makes learners use structure.
answer_key: Guard cell: 'This is a guard cell (claim) because it is kidney-shaped and has a thick inner wall (evidence), which means it can change shape to open or close the stoma (reasoning).'
Root hair cell: 'This is a root hair cell because it has a long extension, which gives a large surface area to take in water and mineral salts.'
Xylem vessel: 'This is a xylem vessel because it is hollow with a thick lignified wall, so water can flow through it.'
Phloem sieve tube: 'This is a phloem sieve tube because it has holes in its end plates, so sugar can pass from cell to cell.'
Palisade cell: 'This is a palisade cell because it is tall and packed with chloroplasts, so it can carry out a lot of photosynthesis.'

slides.title: Four ideas to clear up
slides.subtitle: First we ask why. Then we name the idea.
slides.time_note: Short teacher explanation, with questions

items: droplet :: Why do xylem cells die to work?
link :: What does lignin do in the xylem wall?
arrow_right :: How does sugar pass through sieve plates?
leaf :: Why are palisade cells full of chloroplasts?

do: Take the four tiles one at a time. Ask the question first. Take two or three answers.
Then give a short explanation (see science note).
Link each cell back to the driving question and the healing cut.
say: Why would a cell that is empty inside be good for carrying water? Then we call this idea specialisation.
The cell gave up its living contents so water can flow through the hollow tube.
Lignin is the hard material in the wall of the xylem. It makes the wall strong.
The sieve plates are like holes between rooms. They let sugar flow from cell to cell.
More chloroplasts means more light is caught. That means a faster rate of photosynthesis.
look_for: Learners link each idea to a feature they drew.
Listen for learners using 'specialised' correctly.
if_then: If learners say 'xylem is alive', say: 'Look at your drawing. Where is the nucleus? Where is the cytoplasm?'
If learners confuse xylem and phloem, say: 'Xylem carries water. Phloem carries sugar. Which one has holes in the end plates?'
notes.why_this_works: Asking the question first makes learners think before they hear the answer, so the explanation has something to attach to. This addresses the misconception that dead cells cannot be useful.
notes.science_note: Xylem vessels develop from living cells; the cell contents break down and lignin strengthens the wall, leaving a hollow tube. Sieve plates are the perforated end walls of phloem sieve tube elements.

slides.title: Is the xylem vessel alive?
slides.subtitle: Use evidence from today.
slides.time_note: Think, take 3 answers, then write one sentence

blocks.text: The xylem vessel has no nucleus and no cytoplasm. Is it still a cell? Does it still count as specialised?
Write one sentence: Is the xylem vessel alive?
items: The xylem vessel is … because …

do: Ask the question aloud. Wait 15 seconds. Take 3 responses.
Then everyone writes one sentence in their notebook. Collect the notebooks or slips as an exit-check.
say: The xylem vessel is dead. No nucleus, no cytoplasm.
Is it still a cell? Does it still count as specialised?
Now write one sentence: Is the xylem vessel alive? Use evidence from today.
look_for: Read at least 8 sentences. Does the sentence say it is not alive and use evidence (no nucleus, no cytoplasm, hollow)?
Listen for 'it was a living cell that became specialised'.
if_then: If a learner writes 'it is alive because it carries water', say: 'Carrying water is its job. What do living cells have inside them that this one does not?'
If a learner says it is not a cell, say: 'It started as a living cell. What did it give up to do its job?'
notes.why_this_works: Writing an answer that must cite evidence shows each learner's thinking, not just the loudest voice. It targets the misconception that every working cell must be alive.
answer_key: The xylem vessel is not alive because it has no nucleus and no living cytoplasm. It started as a living cell and is still a specialised cell, because its hollow lumen and lignified wall let water flow through.

slides.title: Back to our predictions
slides.subtitle: Who was closest? What surprised us?
slides.time_note: Mark your own predictions in a new colour

items: check :: Tick the ideas you got right
cross :: Mark the ideas that were different
pencil :: Write the correct idea in a new colour

blocks.text: Who was closest? What did we get right, and what surprised us?

do: Point to the 'BEFORE — Our Predictions' columns on the board.
Learners mark their own notebook predictions in a different colour pen or pencil.
Take 2 or 3 comments from learners about what they got right and what surprised them.
say: Look back at the predictions on the board.
Who was closest? What did we get right, and what surprised us?
Mark your own ideas in a different colour. Wrong ideas are useful, because they show us what we learnt.
look_for: Check 6 notebooks: predictions are marked in a different colour and one corrected idea is written.
Listen for learners who explain why they changed their idea.
if_then: If a learner will not mark anything wrong, say: 'Compare your leaf cell with the palisade cell. What is the same, and what is different?'
If a learner marks everything wrong, say: 'Look again. Did your root cell have a long shape? That part may be right.'
notes.why_this_works: Marking their own predictions shows learners how far their thinking has moved. Common misconception: being wrong is a failure; the new colour shows it as learning.
answer_key: Model answer: 'I predicted a long, thin root cell and a green leaf cell. I was right that the root cell is long and thin, because the root hair cell has a long extension. I was surprised that the xylem vessel is empty inside.'

slides.title: Driving Question Board: two slips
slides.subtitle: Write one new question and one connection.
slides.time_note: Two slips in 2 minutes

blocks.text: A classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes with small gold stars beside some of them.
items: dqb_sticky_notes_board
A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes, with three small gold stars stuck beside some notes, and a wooden desk with a pot of pencils in front.
question :: Slip 1 (New Questions): one question from today
link :: Slip 2 (Growing Answers): how today connects to the cut finger

do: Give each learner two sticky notes or paper slips.
Slip 1 is a new question that today's lesson raised. Slip 2 is one connection to the wound-healing phenomenon.
After 2 minutes, collect slips and place them on the Driving Question Board in the zones 'New Questions' and 'Growing Answers'.
Afterwards, sort the connection slips into 'strong link' (names cells and mechanisms) and 'developing link' (general statements).
say: Two slips. Two minutes.
First slip: a question this lesson made you want to ask.
Second slip: one way today's plant cells connect back to the cut finger.
look_for: Check at least 8 slips. A strong connection slip names a specific cell and a substance or process.
A developing slip is general, such as 'plants and animals are living things'. Use this to plan differentiation for Lesson 10.
if_then: If a slip is general, say: 'Name a cell and a substance. What does that cell make or move? How could that reach the cut finger?'
If a learner has no question, say: 'What would you want to ask about guard cells in a drought?'
notes.why_this_works: Writing a question and a connection makes learners look for links between plant cells and the cut finger. The common misconception is that plant biology is separate from the healing cut.
answer_key: Model question: 'If guard cells control water loss, what happens to a maize plant in Turkana during a drought? Do the guard cells ever stay closed?'
Model connection: 'Just like fibroblasts rebuilt skin, the phloem carries sugars that give energy. So plant cells and animal cells are connected in keeping us alive.'

slides.title: Which question should we answer first?
slides.subtitle: Vote by a show of hands.
slides.time_note: Read 3 questions, vote, then count Lesson 1 questions we can now answer

blocks.text: Which question do you most want us to answer before the end of this unit?

items: raised_hand :: Hands up for each question we read out
hourglass :: Count the Lesson 1 questions we can now answer

do: Read 3 questions from the 'New Questions' zone aloud.
Ask for a show of hands for each. Tally the hands where everyone can see.
Point to the 'Growing Answers' zone and the questions from Lesson 1. Count how many the class can now answer.
Choose 2 or 3 Lesson 1 questions that today's cells help to answer.
say: By a show of hands, which of these three questions do you most want us to answer before the end of this unit?
Look at the questions we posted in Lesson 1. How many can we now answer? Let's count.
Our driving question asks why cells look different and how shape determines job. Today we added five more examples. The pattern is becoming clear. Let's see if it holds all the way to Lesson 12.
look_for: The tally is visible on the board for all three questions.
Learners can name a Lesson 1 question that today's lesson helps to answer. Ask 4 learners.
Listen for learners using something they saw today as evidence.
if_then: If no one can link to a Lesson 1 question, say: 'Read one question from Lesson 1 out loud. Which of today's cells helps us answer it?'
If votes split evenly, say: 'We will keep all three on the board and answer them in order.'
notes.why_this_works: Counting answered questions makes progress visible and builds confidence. It keeps the Driving Question Board a working tool, not a wall display.

slides.title: Model: add the Plant Side
slides.subtitle: Use a new colour. Add all five plant cells.
slides.time_note: Add the plant side with arrows

items: pencil :: Draw and label all five plant cells
magnifier :: Add each cell's feature and function
arrow_right :: Add arrows to show which cells work together
memo :: Write: This model is based on evidence from …

do: Learners open their cumulative Cell Specialisation Model. It shows specialised animal cells around the wound-healing phenomenon.
They add a 'Plant Side' in a new colour.
Each plant cell needs a labelled diagram, its key structural feature and its function.
Learners add arrows: in the root (root hair cells absorb, then xylem transports); in the leaf (palisade cells photosynthesise, phloem exports sugars, guard cells regulate water loss).
Circulate and check models.
say: Open your cumulative model. Today you add a Plant Side, in a new colour.
Every cell must have: a labelled diagram, its key structural feature, and its function.
Then draw arrows to show which cells work together: in the root, and in the leaf.
look_for: Check 6 models: all five plant cells with labelled structural features (not just names).
Arrows between cells show how they work together, and the evidence sentence is written.
if_then: If a learner draws only cell names, say: 'Which feature of this cell tells us its job? Draw it and label it.'
If arrows are missing, say: 'Which cell passes water or sugar on to which cell? Show it with an arrow.'
notes.why_this_works: Revising one model in a new colour each lesson shows how thinking grows. Common misconception: plant and animal specialisation are unrelated; one shared model shows the same pattern.
answer_key: Model: five labelled drawings (root hair cell, guard cells, xylem vessel, phloem sieve tube, palisade cell), each with a feature and a function. Root arrows: root hair cells absorb water and mineral salts, then xylem transports them. Leaf arrows: palisade cells photosynthesise, then phloem exports sugars; guard cells regulate water loss. Evidence sentence: 'This model is based on evidence from the cell diagrams and the Turkana and Kericho stomata.'

slides.title: Model: add one bridge arrow
slides.subtitle: Draw one bridge arrow to the cut finger. Name what flows.
slides.time_note: Draw one bridge arrow and label it

blocks.text: A plate of githeri with sukuma wiki on a wooden table beside a jiko.
items: githeri_sukuma_plate
A friendly flat cartoon of a wooden table in a Kenyan kitchen holding a plate of githeri with a side of green sukuma wiki, a wooden mwiko and a charcoal jiko with a sufuria in the background.

blocks.text: What does the plant give to the animal side?

do: Learners draw one bridge arrow from the plant side to the animal wound-healing side.
The arrow must name a substance, such as glucose, water or mineral salts.
Offer this sentence starter if needed: '… cells make … which gives … to …'.
Circulate and prompt struggling learners.
At the end of the lesson, photograph 4 or 5 models to check depth of systems thinking before Lesson 10.
say: Draw one bridge arrow to the animal side.
What does the plant give the animal?
Think about what fibroblasts need to do their job. Where does that energy come from, all the way back?
look_for: Check 6 models: at least one bridge arrow that names a specific substance flowing from plant to animal.
Listen for mechanism, not just 'plants help animals'.
if_then: If a learner has no idea, say: 'Think about what fibroblasts need to make collagen. Where does that energy come from, all the way back?'
If the bridge is only 'plants and animals are living things', say: 'Name the cell and the substance it makes or moves.'
notes.why_this_works: The bridge arrow makes learners connect plant processes to animal healing through a real flow of matter or energy. It targets the idea that plant cells have nothing to do with the cut finger.
answer_key: Model bridge arrow: 'Palisade cells make glucose via photosynthesis, and glucose powers fibroblasts to make collagen.'

slides.title: Share your bridge arrow
slides.subtitle: Tell your partner. Then predict what comes next.
slides.time_note: Partner share, 2 explanations to the class, then one sentence

items: people :: Share your bridge arrow with your partner
speech :: Two learners explain their bridge to the class
pencil :: Write one sentence: what do you think we will learn next lesson?

do: Learners share their bridge arrow with a partner.
Cold-call 2 learners to explain their bridge in two sentences. Choose one with a strong bridge and one whose bridge needed support.
Learners write a one-sentence prediction for the next lesson in their notebook.
Close with the teacher's final words.
say: Show us your bridge arrow and explain it in two sentences.
Now write one sentence: what do you think we will learn next lesson?
In Lesson 1 we asked: why does the cut finger heal? Today we found that the answer involves not just animal cells but plant cells too.
Every meal of githeri or sukuma wiki that feeds our body's repair workers is made possible by specialised plant cells doing their jobs perfectly. That is the power of cell specialisation.
look_for: Listen for bridge explanations that name a cell and a substance. Cold-call 2 learners.
Check 5 notebooks: the prediction sentence links to what was learnt today.
if_then: If an explanation is vague, say: 'Which cell? Which substance? Where does it go?'
If a learner cannot predict, say: 'Think about how the cells in the root and leaf worked together. What might be the next question?'
notes.why_this_works: Explaining a link aloud and predicting the next step makes learners use their model to think ahead. It keeps the unit story moving from one lesson to the next.
answer_key: Model prediction: 'I predict we will learn how cells join together to form bigger parts of the body, because cells in the root and leaf worked together today.'

build_log.sow_says: Observe: about 6 minutes per cell for five cells (about 30 minutes) plus the Turkana/Kericho comparison and a 3-learner cold-call. Explain: 8-minute card match, 90-second CER presentations, 10-minute mini-lecture, written check and prediction review. DQB: 2 minutes of slips plus a 4-minute discussion. Model Building: 12 minutes plus cold-calls. SoW total is about 100 minutes (estimated, because some parts have no stated time).
build_log.deck_does: Fits 80 minutes: Predict 8, Observe 26, Explain 25, Driving Question Board 5, Model Building 12, with 1 minute for the unit map, 1 for goals and 2 for the Summary Table. Cells take 3-4 minutes each instead of 6. The mini-lecture is 6 minutes instead of 10. The Driving Question Board discussion is 3 minutes instead of 4.
build_log.why: The SoW activities add up to more than 80 minutes. Times were cut across all phases without removing any activity. Observe and Model Building lose slightly more than a quarter, so the teacher checker should confirm the pace is realistic.

build_log.deck_does: Completes the set. Function cards: F1 Carries water up the plant (xylem). F2 Makes food by photosynthesis (palisade). lesson_oneliner: Do plant cells specialise too? Find out how shape fits job in a bean seedling.
purpose: Learners discover that plant cells specialise just as animal cells do.
They study five cells: root hair cell, guard cell, xylem vessel, phloem sieve tube and palisade mesophyll cell.
They see that each cell's structure suits its job, and that plant cells work together in systems.
They link plant cell specialisation to the cut finger. This keeps the driving question alive: how does shape decide a cell's job?
before_class: Place the class bean seedling at the front where everyone can see it.
Check that no learner has a legume allergy before anyone handles bean material. Learners wash their hands afterwards.
Store microscope slides from earlier lessons safely away before the card activity.
Prepare 15 cards per group of four: 5 unlabelled cell diagram cards, 5 function cards (F1 to F5) and 5 place cards (C1 to C5). The card text is on the Match the cards slide.
Prepare two images of stomata: a maize leaf from dry Turkana and a tea leaf from humid Kericho. The SoW gives none, so you must supply them.
Prepare name cards for cold-calling, and two sticky notes or paper slips per learner.
Mark two Driving Question Board zones: 'New Questions' and 'Growing Answers'.
Ask learners to bring their cumulative Cell Specialisation Model and pens or pencils in two colours.
do_not_show: Do not show the Cell 1 to Cell 5 diagram slides until Predict is finished and learners have written their own ideas.
Do not show the Turkana and Kericho stomata slide until you have set up the observation table.
Do not show the card answers (F and C matches) at any time. They are in the notes only.
Do not name Lesson 10 ideas (tissues, organs, organ systems) during the lesson. They are the next discovery.
so_far: You have met plant and animal cells and seen how animal cells specialise.
goals: Describe the structure of five specialised plant cells.
Explain how each cell's shape suits its job.
Connect plant cell jobs to the healing cut.

key_words.definition: A cell with a shape that suits one job.
What a cell looks like and what is inside it.
Something you can see or measure.

Match 15 cards; present using Claim, Evidence, Reasoning; xylem check

Notebooks and pens or pencils in two colours

glance.fallback: If card sets are short, groups share a projected set and write the matches in their books. If the seedling is missing, use the drawing on the first slide.

resource_notes.note: General plant versus animal cell comparison covers Lessons 4–5 content and is too basic for specialised cells. Use as revision after Explain, or skip.
General cell biology practice, not about plant specialisation. Check the questions suit Grade 10 and avoid answers; better as revision after the Explain phase.
Overview of generic plant and animal cells repeats Lessons 4–5 and does not show specialised cells. Use as revision after 'Is the xylem vessel alive?' if needed.
Plant cell structures reading may cover organelles rather than the five specialised cells. Check it includes root hair, guard, xylem, phloem or palisade cells before Observe.
Cell wall video links to lignin and thick guard cell walls, but is not specialised-cell focused. Check relevance; best after 'Four ideas to clear up'.
Practice on plant cell structures may only test organelles. Preview for questions on specialised cells; use after the Explain consolidation as a check.
Organelle structure-function exercise is general and does not fit question-writing. Use as revision after the model slides, or in Lesson 11.
General plant cell reading may support the Plant Side diagrams. Check it shows specialised cells and not only organelles before students use it.

summary.observe_prompt: Name the five plant cells and one feature you saw in each.
summary.learn_prompt: Do plant cells specialise? Give one example of structure fitting job.
summary.explain_prompt: Use a bridge arrow to link a plant cell to the cut finger.
summary.next_lesson: How cells join together to build bigger parts of a living thing.
summary.answer_observe: I observed five specialised plant cells. The root hair cell has a long extension and a large vacuole. Guard cells are kidney-shaped with a thick inner wall and chloroplasts. The xylem vessel is hollow with a thick lignified wall. The phloem sieve tube has sieve plates at its ends and a companion cell. The palisade cell is tall and packed with chloroplasts. Stomata were mostly closed in dry Turkana and mostly open in humid Kericho.
summary.answer_learn: Plant cells specialise just as animal cells do. Each cell has a structure that suits its job: the long root hair absorbs water, the hollow lignified xylem carries water, and the many chloroplasts in palisade cells make food by photosynthesis. These cells work together: absorption, transport, photosynthesis and regulation.
summary.answer_explain: Palisade cells make glucose by photosynthesis. Glucose gives energy that ends up powering animal cells such as fibroblasts, which make collagen to rebuild skin. So specialised plant cells help the body to heal the cut finger. The same rule applies everywhere: shape suits job.
reflection: During Match the cards, which cell caused the most wrong matches? If more than one third of groups mismatched xylem or phloem, plan a 5-minute re-teach to open Lesson 10.
Could learners draw real bridge arrows that name a substance? If not, begin Lesson 10 with a think-aloud of your own bridge arrow.
Look at the Growing Answers slips. Were they strong links with cell names and substances, or general statements? Use this to set the depth expected in Lesson 10.
Did learners engage with the Turkana and Kericho comparison, or treat it as decoration? If engagement was low, bring a real leaf from the school compound next time.
Were the timings realistic for your class? Which part ran short?

Read 3 or 4 answers aloud if time allows.

What did you learn about plant cells?

notes.why_this_works: Three linked questions take learners from what they saw to what it means. The last one links back to the anchor phenomenon.

do: Show the unit map. Point to YOU ARE HERE at Lesson 9.
Read the So far line aloud.

Today we ask: does the same rule hold for plants?
Keep the cut finger in mind. We will come back to it.
unit_map_notes.why_this_works: A quick look at the whole unit shows learners where today fits. This links today's lesson to the anchor phenomenon, the healing cut.

do: Read the three goals aloud, one at a time.
Read the four key words and their meanings.
Tell learners they will use the words later. Do not explain them in detail yet.

You can explain how each shape suits its job.

goals_notes.why_this_works: Short goals tell learners what success looks like. The key words are general ones, so they do not give away any answer before learners predict.
